description: Frame into the hips rather than pushing the chest, walk the shoulders back toward the feet, and force the opponent's weight down to low mount before attempting any escape.

description: Turn the thumb toward the opponent's feet, follow the rotation of your own shoulder, and walk around to your knees so the elbow leaves the hyperextension line.

name: Kesa-Gatame Escape
description: Free the trapped arm to the far side of their back, bridge over the near shoulder, and either roll them backwards or sit up into their armpit space.
when_to_use: Use when the opponent turns their chest away and sits into a headlock pin. The pin is strong against the head and weak against a bridge over the shoulder they have turned away from.

source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Underhook Escape to Turtle
description: Win the underhook on the far side, turn onto your knees while keeping the head high, and come up to turtle or straight into a single leg.
when_to_use: Use when the crossface is loose or the opponent is chasing a submission rather than holding the pin. Turning without the underhook gives up the back, so the underhook is the precondition rather than a bonus.

source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Kimura Defence from Bottom Side Control
description: Grip your own belt or thigh to shorten the lever, bring the elbow tight to the ribs, and turn toward the trapped arm rather than away from it.
when_to_use: Use the instant the figure-four closes, before the arm is walked behind the back. Turning away lengthens the lever and finishes the lock for them, which is why the direction of the turn is the whole technique.

name: North-South Escape
description: Frame on the hips, bridge to lift their weight off the chest, and spin the head out to one side to arrive at bottom side control or guard.
when_to_use: Use before the opponent settles their chest onto yours and starts hunting the north-south choke or the kimura. North-south is a transitional pin, so escaping it early is far cheaper than escaping it late.
source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Back Defence Hand Fighting
description: Tuck the chin, keep both hands on the choking arm with a two-on-one, and never let the strangling hand cross the centreline of your neck.
when_to_use: Use immediately on losing the back, before any escape. Survival precedes escape here: an escape attempted while the choking arm is under the chin simply hands over the finish.
source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Shoulder-to-Shoulder Escape
description: Trap the choking arm, walk your shoulders toward the mat on the side away from the danger, and slide the hips down until both hooks are cleared and you land in bottom side control.
when_to_use: Use once the choking arm is controlled and you can pick a side. Escaping toward the choking arm is the common error; going shoulder-to-shoulder on the safe side is what makes it work.
common_counters: Body triangle to stop the slide
source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Body Triangle Escape

description: Turn toward the locked ankle side, peel the top foot down toward your hip, and sit up over the triangle so the lock breaks or slides to the waist.
when_to_use: Use when the opponent replaces hooks with a body triangle, which is far harder to slide out of than hooks. It must be attacked toward the ankle side; turning the other way tightens it.
common_counters: Attack the choke as the turn starts
source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Granby Roll to Guard
description: Roll over the near shoulder while keeping the hips higher than the head, and come out facing the opponent with the legs back between you.
when_to_use: Use from turtle when the opponent is chasing hooks but has not yet secured a seatbelt. The head must stay off the mat throughout, which is the difference between a recovery and giving up the back.

name: Monoplata
description: Trap the arm with one leg over the shoulder while the arm stays in front of your body, sit up onto the hip, and lever the shoulder without needing the second leg.
when_to_use: Use as an armbar or omoplata fails and the arm slips to the near side. It is most valuable as a chain link rather than a primary attack, because the entry is usually a rescued position.
common_counters: Posture and pull the arm free
source_notes: Submission chain curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Baratoplata

when_to_use: Use when a kimura grip is secured but the opponent defends by gripping their own belt or leg. Replacing your hand with the shin beats the grip strength that stalls the plain kimura.

source_notes: Submission chain curriculum; naming varies by academy.

description: Keep elbows inside the knees, hands protecting the collar line, head off the mat, and hips moving so no submission or high mount can settle.
when_to_use: Use as the default the moment you are mounted, before choosing an escape. Every mount escape depends on frames that already exist, so building them is the first move rather than a fallback.
source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Side Control Bottom Frames
description: Place one forearm across the hip and one into the neck or shoulder, keep the near elbow off the mat, and stay on your side rather than flat.

name: Turtle Bottom Survival Posture
description: Keep elbows to knees, head up and off the mat, hands defending the collar and the near-side hook entry, and never let the hips rise above the shoulders.
when_to_use: Use whenever a scramble drops you to turtle. Turtle is a waypoint rather than a destination, so the posture exists to buy the two seconds a Granby or a wrestle-up needs.
source_notes: Bottom-position curriculum; naming varies by academy.

name: Alligator Walk
description: Crawl forward chest-low with elbows and knees wide, driving off alternating hands and feet while the hips stay below shoulder height.
when_to_use: Warm-up staple for the low posture passing demands — the same hip height a smash pass wants is the one this drill grooves. Logged as class content, not a technique.
source_notes: Solo movement drill; category Other like the breakfalls and stance rows.

name: Americana from Closed Guard
description: When they post a hand on the mat beside your head, snake your same-side arm over theirs and grip your own wrist, pinning their wrist to the mat, then bridge slightly into the figure-four to rotate the shoulder.
when_to_use: Use the instant a hand posts on the mat next to you — a posted hand in closed guard is a loan you collect immediately. Rare precisely because the post is a beginner's mistake, which is why beginners should know the punishment.
common_counters: Pull the elbow to the ribs
source_notes: Bottom-side americana; the top-side versions from mount and side control were already here.

name: Ankle Lock from Guard
description: From open guard against a standing opponent, wrap their heel in your armpit as you fall back, pinch your knees around their leg, and arch your hips into the trapped ankle.
when_to_use: Use when their lead foot lingers inside your guard during a pass attempt — falling back onto it is faster than any sweep. The classic first leg attack, and the reason passers are taught to keep their feet moving.
common_next_moves: Secure the new guard or entanglement
source_notes: The guard-entry straight ankle; the four existing ankle-lock rows all start inside entanglements.

name: Arm Triangle from Back
description: When they turn into your seatbelt to escape, keep the over-arm wrapped past their neck and shoulder, let them come chest-to-chest, and finish the head-and-arm squeeze from the top or knees.
when_to_use: Use when they win the turn — the seatbelt arm that failed to choke the back becomes the arm triangle the moment their shoulder line rotates into it. The escape and the choke share a doorway; you are standing in it.
source_notes: Known as the Canto choke; the planned back-escape counter to teach beside the escapes.

name: Arm-Wrap Guard Control
description: From closed guard, wrap one of their arms to your own chest with both of yours — palm-to-palm behind their triceps — and hug it flat so their posture and their base post disappear together.
when_to_use: Use against a no-gi posture built on a chest post — wrapping the posting arm deletes the post and the pressure with it. The wrapped side's back take and the pendulum to the far side are the standing threats.
common_counters: Pull the elbow to the ribs
source_notes: No-gi closed-guard control beside the overhook and high-elbow rows.

name: Armbar to Rear Naked Choke Chain
description: Attack the armbar from back control by climbing the legs over the shoulder; when they clasp their hands to defend, return to the choke the defence uncrossed, and alternate until one lands.
when_to_use: Use when neither attack finishes alone: the hand position that defends the choke feeds the armbar and the one that defends the armbar exposes the neck. Chain rows exist for logging the pair as it is actually drilled.
source_notes: Mirrors the existing Armbar–Triangle–Omoplata Chain convention, from the back instead of guard.

name: Ashi Guruma
description: Enter as for a hip throw but keep your hips off theirs, wheeling them over a straight leg placed across their shin line while the hands drive the turn.
when_to_use: Use against an opponent who blocks the hip contact harai goshi needs — ashi guruma throws over the leg alone, so their hip defence defends nothing. Timing-heavy; the leg is a pivot, never a kick.
source_notes: The no-hip-contact wheel of the harai goshi family.

name: Backward Roll
description: Sit back and roll over one shoulder — never the head — letting the momentum carry your legs over so you finish on your knees or feet facing the way you came.
when_to_use: The falling skill behind every inversion and granby: going backward over a shoulder on purpose is what makes going backward under pressure safe. Pairs with the forward shoulder roll already recorded.
source_notes: Completes the ukemi set beside the forward roll and the two breakfalls.

name: Banana Split
description: From the truck, lace one of their legs with your legs in a lockdown while gripping the other leg behind the knee with both arms, then extend your body to draw the legs apart.
when_to_use: Use from the truck when the twister's neck entry is defended — the legs are already split and the submission is the position finished honestly. Groin-stretch tap: apply slowly, because it goes from uncomfortable to injurious quickly.
source_notes: The truck's third attack, beside the calf slicer and twister already here.

name: Baseball-Bat Choke from Mount
description: Set the palm-up and palm-down collar grips from mount, then dismount toward north-south around the pinned shoulder, letting the body rotation close the bat as you land.
when_to_use: Use when they defend the cross-collar choke by chasing your second hand — the bat grips look identical one beat earlier. Giving up mount for it is real, which is why it works: nobody expects the choke that costs you four points.
source_notes: The rotation-finish variant of the mount collar chokes.

name: Baseball Choke from Back
description: From back control, set the palm-up and palm-down collar grips, then let them escape their hips and turn — the rotation they use to face you closes the bat.
when_to_use: Use as a trap when your bow-and-arrow grip is repeatedly stripped: the bat grips survive the turn the bow-and-arrow does not. You concede the escape on purpose and collect the choke it walks into.
source_notes: The gi answer to the turning back escape; pairs with the arm triangle's no-gi version of the same trap.

name: Boa Constrictor
description: From a front headlock, feed the choking arm under the neck and behind the far armpit, grip your own biceps, and roll them over the trapped-arm side, letting the roll wind the choke tight.
when_to_use: Use when the anaconda's grip will not close because their far arm posts wide — the boa takes a shallower wrap and lets the roll supply the depth the grip lacked. An anaconda for long-armed defenders.
source_notes: Anaconda-family variant; niche but distinct in grip depth and roll direction.

name: Bow and Arrow Choke from Guard
description: With a deep cross-collar grip, grab their same-side pant leg or ankle with your free hand, swing your leg over their back, and pull collar and leg apart like drawing a bow.
when_to_use: Use when the cross-collar choke's second grip is repeatedly blocked — the bow-and-arrow takes the pant grip they were not defending. The geometry is the back-control version's, borrowed early.
source_notes: The guard-side entry to a choke the library records from back control and technical mount.

name: Bridge Drill (Upa)
description: Lying on your back with feet planted close to your hips, drive the hips as high as they go while turning over one shoulder, reaching across your body to finish facing the mat.
when_to_use: The solo rehearsal of every mount and side-control escape in this library — the trap-and-roll is this drill with somebody on top. Height first, then the turn; a low bridge moves nobody.
source_notes: Solo movement drill; the named escapes it feeds are cross-linked.

name: Bulldog Choke
description: From a side headlock on a turtled or scrambling opponent, wrap the neck with the near arm, clasp your hands, and drive forward while dragging them down so your forearm blades across the carotid.
when_to_use: Use in the scramble when they try to run out the back of a front headlock and give up the side of the neck. It looks crude and works through pressure and direction rather than a lock; win the angle first or it is just a headlock.
source_notes: Scramble choke popularised in MMA; legality follows ordinary choke rules.

name: Butterfly Triangle
description: When your butterfly sweep entry makes them post an arm on the mat or your chest, elevate with the opposite hook while shooting the same-side leg over their shoulder, and fall back into the triangle.
when_to_use: Use against the sweep defence — the posted arm that saves their balance is the arm outside your triangle. Butterfly's attacks come in pairs: they concede the sweep or feed the neck, and this is the neck half.
source_notes: The submission arm of the butterfly sweep dilemma; 24 butterfly rows existed with no triangle.

name: Cement Mixer
description: From a front headlock with a chin strap and far-armpit grip, roll them over their far shoulder by driving your chest and pulling the chin strap through, following the roll to land in side control or a scarf hold.
when_to_use: Use when the turtle is tight enough that the D'Arce and anaconda will not feed but the head and far arm are both controlled — the roll takes what the chokes could not. Funk-wrestling staple that converts a stuck front headlock into a pin.
source_notes: Wrestling import; both the takedown-section and turtle-section requests resolve to this one row.

name: Collar Drag from Seated Guard
aliases: Collar drag back take from guard
description: From seated guard with a cross-collar grip, yank the collar past your hip as you sit through to the outside, coming up chest-to-back before they can square up.
when_to_use: Use the moment they kneel or reach into your seated guard with their weight forward — the drag converts their entry into your back exposure. If they base out mid-drag, you come up on a single leg instead and it is still your exchange.
source_notes: The gi mirror of the butterfly arm drag already in the library.

name: Coyote Half Guard Control
description: Play half guard on your knees rather than your back: underhook deep, head driving into their chest, trapped leg lacing theirs, so you are wrestling from half guard rather than surviving in it.
when_to_use: Use as a standing-start half guard game against opponents who flatten ordinary half — the kneeling posture means there is nothing to flatten. Its exits are the dogfight, the back and the knee tap, all already in this library.
source_notes: Lucas Leite's system; a posture for the half-guard rows rather than a new move set.

name: Crucifix Collar Choke
description: From the crucifix with both their arms trapped, feed your top hand into the far collar palm-down and slide the forearm across the neck, finishing with a slow pull since neither of their hands can help.
when_to_use: Use in the gi where the rear naked choke's arm-position is awkward from the crucifix — the collar does the same work with half the grip fighting. Their arms are the position's whole point: nothing defends the neck.
source_notes: The gi finish beside the existing no-gi crucifix RNC.

name: De La Riva Omoplata
description: With the De La Riva hook and a same-side sleeve grip, kick your free leg through between their legs as you invert slightly, swinging it over the gripped arm's shoulder into the omoplata.
when_to_use: Use when they turn their hips away to kill the DLR hook — the turn presents the near shoulder to the leg you kick through. Sleeve control is the whole trick: without it the arm follows them out.
source_notes: Standard DLR attack absent from an otherwise deep DLR set.

name: De La Riva Triangle
description: Pull them forward onto your hips with the collar grip as the DLR hook lifts, then swap the hook for a leg over the shoulder and lock the triangle as they fall into you.
when_to_use: Use against a posture that leans forward into your collar grip to smash the guard — the lean shortens the distance your legs need. The DLR hook's lift is what turns their step into an entry.
source_notes: Completes the DLR attack pair with the omoplata.

name: Deep-Half Back Take
description: From deep half, off-balance them forward over your head, then spin out the back door between their legs and climb their hips before they can turn to face you.
when_to_use: Use when they base heavily forward to stop the deep-half sweeps — the weight that stops the sweep opens the back door behind it. Deep half's third answer: sweep them backward, roll them over, or leave out the back.
source_notes: Completes deep half's option set beside the Homer Simpson and waiter sweeps.

name: Dogfight Control
description: From the underhook half guard, come up to your knees beside them with your underhook deep and your head outside, both players kneeling hip-to-hip — hold your whizzer-side elbow tight and your base wide.
when_to_use: Use as the staging position the underhook buys you: from the dogfight the knee tap, the limp arm and the back take all launch, and their only good answer is the whizzer. Named rows for its exits already exist; this is the room they leave from.
source_notes: The control row for a named position three existing techniques exit from.

name: 50/50 Sweep
description: From 50/50, grip their collar or wrist to kill their posts, then tilt them over their entangled hip with your legs and follow through to come up on top still inside the 50/50.
when_to_use: Use whenever you are the one underneath in 50/50 — in the gi especially, being the top player in this position is most of the battle. The sweep is won with the hands first: a player with no posts cannot resist a tilt.
source_notes: The basic tilt; the existing 50/50 sweep row covers the stand-up exit instead.

name: Toe Hold from 50/50
description: From 50/50, grip the far foot with a figure-four — hand over the toes, other hand under their ankle gripping your own wrist — and turn the toes toward their knee line to finish.
when_to_use: Use in the gi where the heel hook is off the table — the toe hold is 50/50's legal finish for brown and black belts, and the reason gi players still enter the position at all. Hunt it while they hand-fight your collar grips.
source_notes: The gi finish for a position that had only no-gi heel hooks recorded.

name: Gogoplata from Closed Guard
description: From a broken-down posture with an overhook, feed your shin across their throat under the chin, grip your own instep or their head, and pull the head down onto the shin to choke.
when_to_use: Use when the omoplata hip flexibility is there but they hide the far arm — the gogoplata takes the neck with the same leg the omoplata would use on the shoulder. High guard and rubber guard players get it as a free follow-up.
source_notes: Flexibility-dependent; commonly taught out of rubber guard's mission control.

name: Gogoplata from Mount
description: From high mount, slide one shin across the throat as you climb past their armpit line, sit toward that side, and pull their head up into the shin with both hands.
when_to_use: Use from a high mount where they defend the collar with crossed forearms — the shin goes over the top of the defence rather than through it. Rare, but the mechanics are the mounted triangle's cousin.
source_notes: High-mount variant; the S-mount climb is the common entry.

name: Gogoplata from North–South
description: From north-south with their arms pinned above the head, slide a shin under the chin across the throat, drop your hips, and finish by drawing their head up into the shin.
when_to_use: Use when the north-south choke grip is defended by a chin tuck — the shin enters from above the head where the chin cannot block it. A rarity that exists because the arm-pin from north-south leaves the neck alone undefended.
source_notes: Uncommon; included to complete the gogoplata family alongside the closed-guard and mount entries.

name: Gubber Guard Control
description: Feed their far lapel under their near arm and grip it cross-handed from closed or seated guard, binding their posture to your grip hand so they carry their own restraint.
when_to_use: Use to immobilise a posture-and-pressure passer in the gi — the fed lapel does the holding your arms would otherwise spend themselves on. A lapel-guard entry point beside the worm and squid rows already here.
source_notes: Minor lapel guard recorded beside worm and squid; the curriculum listed it explicitly.

name: Half-Guard Sit-Up Sweep
description: From half guard with the trapped leg laced, sit up sharply into them, reach past the far hip for the mat or their belt, and drive your chest through to topple them over the trapped side.
when_to_use: Use when they sit tall in your half guard to hunt the crossface — the sit-up meets them before the crossface lands. If they post to stop the sweep, the underhook and back are there instead; the sweep's job is to force that choice.
source_notes: The hip-bump's half-guard sibling; distinct from the underhook and dogfight series already here.

name: Hane Goshi
description: Turn in with collar and sleeve grips as for a hip throw, but lift them with a bent leg sprung across both of their thighs while the hip carries the load.
when_to_use: Use when uchi mata's leg-between-legs entry is blocked by a defensive square stance — hane goshi's leg lies across the front and needs no gap. The spring replaces the sweep.
source_notes: Completes the hip-throw set beside harai goshi, o goshi, koshi guruma and uchi mata.

name: Harai Tsurikomi Ashi
description: Pull them upward and forward with the sleeve and collar as if to load a throw, then sweep their advancing foot before it lands, wheeling them over the blocked leg.
when_to_use: Use when sasae's static block keeps missing — harai tsurikomi ashi sweeps the moving foot instead of blocking it, so it beats opponents who step short to defend sasae.
source_notes: The sweeping sibling of the sasae already recorded.

name: Heel Hook Defense
description: Hide the heel by pointing the toes and flexing the foot into a boot, hand-fight their gripping hand off the heel, then turn your knee toward the pressure and spin your body in the direction of the twist until the leg slips clear.
when_to_use: Use the instant the heel is exposed and always before the grip fully closes — a caught heel is answered by rotation toward the twist, never away, because running from the turn is what tears knees. Position over panic: clear the knee line first, the foot second.
common_next_moves: Secure the new guard or entanglement
source_notes: The library's first defensive leg-entanglement row; 26 attacking rows preceded it.

name: High-Elbow Guard Control
description: From closed guard, overhook one arm and climb your grip until your elbow points past their shoulder line, your forearm barring their neck, forcing their head below your chest.
when_to_use: Use in no-gi where the collar grips that break posture do not exist — the high elbow is the no-gi collar. Everything the overhook guard threatens starts a rung higher and arrives a beat faster from here.
source_notes: No-gi posture-control refinement of the overhook guard already recorded.

name: Inversion to Leg Lock
description: From open guard, roll back over your shoulder under their base, threading a leg between theirs mid-inversion so you surface already wrapped around a leg in ashi garami.
when_to_use: Use when they stand wide and heavy to smash-pass — the inversion goes under the pressure rather than against it, and their planted leg cannot retreat while it is bearing weight. The modern bridge between guard retention and the leg-lock game.
setup_from: Reverse De La Riva Kiss of the Dragon
common_next_moves: Secure the new guard or entanglement
source_notes: The inversion entry that links the retention rows to the entanglement rows.

name: Japanese Necktie
description: From a front headlock with the choking arm under the neck and your hand clasped over their far triceps, fall to the choking-arm side, hook the near leg over their back, and crunch to finish.
when_to_use: Use when the D'Arce is half-in but you cannot feed the arm deep enough to lock it — the Japanese necktie finishes from the shallower grip by falling to the opposite side the D'Arce would. A turtle that keeps the far elbow tight is exactly the turtle this beats.
source_notes: The missing sibling of the Peruvian necktie already in the library.

name: Kimura from Mount
description: When they push up into your chest or turn to their side, catch the wrist to the mat, feed your other hand under the elbow to lock the figure-four, then step over their head and rotate the arm behind their back.
when_to_use: Use against the push-and-turn escape attempt — the arm that pushes is the arm you lock. From low mount the kimura also converts a half-successful bridge into a finish, because the turn they wanted feeds the rotation.
source_notes: Fills the one position the kimura family was missing; kimura exists from five other positions in this library.

name: Kimura Sweep from Closed Guard
description: With the kimura figure-four locked, sit toward the trapped arm's side and use the shoulder as a steering wheel to roll them over it, following through to land in mount with the grip still set.
when_to_use: Use when they defend the kimura by gripping their own belt — you cannot rotate the shoulder but you can rotate the whole person around it. The finish waits for you on top with the grip already in hand.
common_counters: Release the belt grip and posture
source_notes: Closes the hip-bump/kimura/guillotine triangle from the kimura corner.

name: Kimura-Trap Half-Guard Pass
description: When they dig for the underhook in half guard, catch the diving arm in a kimura grip, lock it to your chest, and use the control to flatten them while your legs walk the trapped knee free.
when_to_use: Use against a committed underhook attempt — the kimura grip converts their best bottom-half weapon into your handle. The pass and the submission threaten together: defend the shoulder and the leg walks free, defend the leg and the shoulder rotates.
common_next_moves: Kimura-Trap Back Take from Side Control
source_notes: A rare top-game addition to a bottom-heavy catalog; links into the existing kimura-trap back take.

name: Armbar from Knee-on-Belly
aliases: Arm bar from knee on belly
description: When the bottom player pushes the knee with the far arm, trap that arm at the wrist, step the posted foot over their head, and sit back into the armbar with their thumb pointing up.
when_to_use: Use the moment they push on your knee — the push is the armbar. The pressure of the position creates the extended arm; you are not hunting it, you are waiting for it.
source_notes: The classic knee-on-belly reaction attack; taught wherever knee on belly is taught.

name: Baseball-Bat Choke from Knee-on-Belly
aliases: Baseball choke from knee on belly
description: Set a palm-up grip deep in the near collar and a palm-down grip below it, then drop your head to the mat past their far shoulder and let the rotation of your body close the bat.
when_to_use: Use while they are focused on the knee — the grips look like posture control until you spin, and by then the choke is already structurally finished. Works best set early and sprung late.
source_notes: Signature knee-on-belly gi choke; the knee-on-belly entry hides the grips better than the side-control version.

name: Knee-on-Belly Control
description: Post the near knee across the belly below the ribs, keep the other leg long and posted wide, and stay tall with your hips over the knee so your weight rides on them rather than the mat.
when_to_use: Use as a mobile scoring control the moment side control feels settled — it is deliberately uncomfortable, so the bottom player moves and hands you the mount, the back, or an arm. Do not treat it as a pin: the value is the reaction it forces.
source_notes: First resident technique of the knee-on-belly glossary position; previously only a transition destination.

name: Cross-Collar Choke from Knee-on-Belly
aliases: Cross choke from knee on belly
description: Feed the first hand palm-up deep behind the near collar, cross the second palm-down into the far collar as they defend the knee, and drop your chest while flaring the elbows to finish.
when_to_use: Use when both of their hands are busy pushing on your knee and shin — the collars are undefended exactly while the position hurts most. If they release the knee to defend the choke, take mount instead.
source_notes: Standard gi attack from knee on belly; pairs with the mount transition as a dilemma.

name: Elbow-Push Knee-on-Belly Escape
description: Turn onto your side toward them, frame the near forearm across the knee-side shin and the other hand on the knee itself, then hip-escape away as you push the shin past your hip line to insert a knee.
when_to_use: Use immediately — every second under knee on belly costs energy and invites the collar. Push the SHIN, never the thigh, and never with straight arms across your own centre line, because the straight push is exactly what the armbar upstairs is waiting for.
source_notes: The safe-arm-structure escape; the armbar row opposite is what punishes doing it wrong.

name: Knee-on-Belly Sit-to-Guard Escape
description: As the knee lands, sit up sharply into their base before the weight settles, posting on the far elbow and wedging the near forearm inside the knee to slide your hips out and face them in seated guard.
when_to_use: Use in the first beat of the position, before they are heavy — knee on belly is lightest the moment it is placed. Late, the sit-up feeds the baseball choke; early, it turns their two points into your guard.
common_next_moves: Secure the new guard or entanglement
source_notes: Timing-based counter to the knee ride; the pair with the elbow-push escape covers early and late.

name: Knee-on-Belly to Mount
description: From the knee ride, windshield-wiper the posted knee across their belly or step the posted foot over the far hip, then drop your hips into mount before their elbow can insert.
when_to_use: Use when their elbows chase your knee-on-belly and leave the far hip line open. The step-over is safest while they are mid-push — their frames are pointed at the knee, not the mount.
source_notes: The standard scoring ladder out of the knee ride; two points into four.

name: Triangle from Knee-on-Belly
description: When they push the knee with the near arm, catch the wrist, step your posted leg over their head, and drop your hips onto their shoulder line to lock the triangle from top.
when_to_use: Use against a straight-arm push across their own centre line — the push puts one arm in and one arm out for you. A committed push is a triangle; a frame on the hip is the armbar instead.
source_notes: The mounted-triangle entry that starts from the knee ride rather than mount.

name: Knee-Shield Omoplata
description: When they cross-face over your knee shield, swing the shield leg over their near shoulder as you invert slightly under them, catching the arm and sitting up into the omoplata as they fall forward.
when_to_use: Use when the triangle's angle is blocked by their posture but the near arm is committed to your body — the omoplata takes the shoulder the crossface volunteered. Pairs with the knee-shield triangle as an either-arm dilemma.
source_notes: Second half of the knee-shield attack pair.

name: Knee-Shield Triangle
description: When they reach past your knee shield to control your head or collar, shoot the shield-side leg over that shoulder, cut an angle with your hips, and lock the triangle with the trapped half-guard leg freed to close it.
when_to_use: Use against the reach — a knee shield forces them to lean through it to reach you, and the lean puts their head and one arm inside your legs. The knee shield's first submission, and the reason passing it flat-armed is wrong.
source_notes: First attack for the knee-shield position; control and recovery rows existed without any offence.

name: Kneebar from Guard Top
description: From inside their open or half-open guard, backstep over one of their thighs, sit onto it with their kneecap at your hip line, and extend their leg between your legs like an armbar.
when_to_use: Use when their guard chases your legs with hooks — the backstep spins their hook into your kneebar. A top-player's counter-attack that makes lazy hook-chasing expensive.
source_notes: Top-side leg attack; the existing kneebars start from saddle and top half guard.

name: Lasso Guard Triangle
description: From a deep lasso, spin under the lassoed arm as you pull the sleeve across, letting the lasso leg slide over the shoulder into the triangle while the sleeve grip keeps the arm inside.
when_to_use: Use when they try to back out of the lasso — pulling away straightens the lassoed arm and the triangle rides it in. The lasso's threats are the sweep if they stay and this if they leave.
source_notes: Joins the existing lasso sweep and omoplata to finish the set.

name: Mantis Guard Control
description: From seated guard, hook one foot behind their lead ankle from the inside while your same-side hand posts behind you, using the low hook to trip them forward or lift into deeper entanglements.
when_to_use: Use against a low, disengaged passer whose ankles are the only thing in range — the mantis hook attacks the one contact point they must give. A doorway guard: everything it wins converts into shin-to-shin or single-leg X.
source_notes: Modern low-hook open guard; recorded as a control row with exits into the existing entanglement set.

name: Morote Seoi Nage
description: Keeping both grips — sleeve and lapel — turn in and jam your lapel-side elbow under their armpit, loading them onto your back for the shoulder throw without ever releasing the collar.
when_to_use: Use when releasing the lapel for ippon seoi's arm-wrap feels unsafe against a strong gripper — morote keeps both hands where they were. The elbow placement is the throw; a high elbow throws nobody.
source_notes: The two-grip seoi; distinct entry mechanics from the ippon and drop versions recorded.

name: Neck Crank (Can Opener)
description: Inside their closed guard, clasp both hands behind their head and pull the chin toward their chest while posturing your own spine up and back.
when_to_use: A pressure tool more than a finish: in rulesets that allow it, the can opener forces a closed guard open because holding the guard while the neck is flexed becomes untenable. Recorded for completeness — spinal cranks without a choke are prohibited in IBJJF competition.
source_notes: Prohibited as a spinal crank in IBJJF; included so logging it is possible where trained, with legality shown honestly.

name: Ninja Choke
description: From a front headlock, reach the choking arm under the neck and grip your other biceps with the second hand behind their far armpit, then sit through toward the far side and curl to finish.
when_to_use: Use when the guillotine hand-position is set but they posture too strongly to fall guard-side — the ninja choke finishes by sitting to the opposite side, using their own posture against them.
source_notes: Front-headlock family; sits between the guillotine and the necktie chokes.

name: Okuri Ashi Barai
description: As they step sideways, sweep their trailing foot into their leading foot with the sole of your foot, timed so both of their feet leave the mat together.
when_to_use: Use against lateral movement — a circling opponent briefly has both feet travelling the same direction and this sweep collects them. Pure timing; strength adds nothing and telegraphing kills it.
source_notes: The travelling version of the de ashi barai already recorded.

name: Omoplata from Back
description: As they clear your second hook and begin to turn away, swing the leg they cleared over their far shoulder and sit through into the omoplata before their escape finishes.
when_to_use: Use as the toll on a half-finished back escape — the shoulder they turn away from you is the shoulder the leg catches. It converts a lost position into a submission, which is the cheapest kind of offence.
source_notes: The omoplata family's back-control exit; punishes the shoulder-to-shoulder escape.

name: Penetration Step
description: Drop your level by bending the knees with the back straight, step deep between an imaginary opponent's feet onto a flat lead foot, and drive through off the trailing leg.
when_to_use: The entry mechanic under every double and single leg in this library — drilled solo so the level change comes from the legs, not the back. A shot that starts with a bent spine ends with a sprawl on your neck.
source_notes: Wrestling fundamental; the takedowns it feeds are cross-linked.

name: Reverse Triangle from Closed Guard
description: When they duck their head to the outside of your hip during a pass attempt, lock your legs in a figure-four around their neck and near arm from the reversed angle and squeeze across the back of the neck.
when_to_use: Use when the ordinary triangle's front entry is gone because their head dropped outside — the reverse triangle takes the same two targets from behind. Mostly arrives uninvited out of stack passes; know it so you recognise the gift.
source_notes: Ura sankaku; the reversed-angle member of the triangle family.

name: Rolling Back Take from Turtle
description: With a seatbelt on the turtle, tuck your head to the mat beside them and roll over your own shoulder, carrying them through the roll so you land behind them with both hooks available.
when_to_use: Use when the turtle is too heavy to break down in place — the roll uses their base against them by taking the ground away. Commit fully: half a roll gives the back away instead of taking it.
source_notes: The dynamic sibling of the chair-sit; covers both rolling-back-take requests in the curriculum.

name: Rolling Kimura
description: From a front headlock on the turtle, lock a kimura grip on their near arm, then roll over your shoulder past their far side, carrying the arm so you land with them in the kimura trap on their back.
when_to_use: Use when the turtle grips their own forearms to block the chin strap — the kimura takes the arm their defence offered. The roll converts a stalled front headlock into a finishing position without ever fighting the head.
common_next_moves: Kimura-Trap Back Take from Side Control
source_notes: Funk-wrestling kimura entry; joins the standing kimura trap and side-control kimura rows.

name: Rubber Guard Matrix
description: From mission control, swim your free arm under your own lasso-side leg to trap their posting arm (New York), then bring the foot across their face to the far shoulder — the matrix — pinning their posture with your leg alone.
when_to_use: Use when mission control holds but the omoplata's arm isolation keeps failing — the matrix ladder wins the arm one rung at a time. Flexibility-dependent like everything in this system.
source_notes: The station between mission control and the finishes; both curriculum aliases point at this one row.

name: Seoi Otoshi
description: Turn in for a shoulder throw but drop to one or both knees under their centre, pulling them over your shoulder line into the space your level change opened.
when_to_use: Use against a taller opponent whose height keeps the standing seoi nage from getting under — the drop manufactures the height difference. Knees take the impact; drill the entry before trusting it.
source_notes: The drop-entry variant beside the standing and drop seoi rows.

name: Shin-on-Shin to Single-Leg X
description: From shin-on-shin with an ankle grip, elevate their leg with your shin as you slide underneath, swapping your outside foot to the hip to arrive in single-leg X under their base.
when_to_use: Use when they stand square in front of your seated guard — shin-on-shin is the knock on the door and single-leg X is the room. The wrestle-up and this entry punish opposite reactions: weight back, wrestle up; weight forward, go under.
common_next_moves: Straight Ankle Lock from Single-Leg X
source_notes: Completes shin-on-shin's option pair beside the existing wrestle-up and knee-tap sweep.

name: Shoulder-Roll Back Escape
description: When their hooks ride high, tuck your chin and roll over your own shoulder in the direction of their choking arm, folding out of the seatbelt through the space behind your own head.
when_to_use: Use only when they overcommit their weight above your shoulder line — the roll needs their mass forward to leave the hooks behind. A rarer, faster exit than the shoulder-to-shoulder slide; wrong against a heavy low hook ride.
source_notes: The dynamic complement to the shoulder-to-shoulder escape already in the library.

name: Spider-Lasso Guard Control
description: Combine one spider foot on the biceps with a lasso wrapped on the other arm, sleeve grips on both, so one side pushes while the other side binds.
when_to_use: Use when plain spider guard keeps losing a foot — the lasso side cannot be shrugged off, which frees the spider side to push and off-balance. The standard gi answer to spider-guard grip strippers.
source_notes: The hybrid configuration behind the lasso attacks already recorded.

name: Standing Collar Drag
description: With a cross-collar grip, snap the collar past your hip as you step your gripping-side foot back and outside, dragging them past you onto their hands so you can front or take the back.
when_to_use: Use against an opponent leaning into their grips — the drag borrows the pressure they are already giving you. In the gi it is the arm drag's stronger cousin, because the collar cannot be limp-armed away.
common_next_moves: Enter a takedown or guard pull
source_notes: Gi staple absent from the catalog despite three curriculum references; the seated version is its own row.

name: Standing Single-Leg X Entry
description: Sit down onto one of their lead legs from standing, sliding your outside foot to their hip while the inside leg hooks behind their knee, arriving in single-leg X before they can sprawl.
when_to_use: Use against a low staredown opponent who will not engage grips — sitting into their lead leg forces the entanglement they were avoiding. The no-gi answer to a stalling standing game.
source_notes: The standing entry the SLX system lacked; butterfly and shin-to-shin entries already exist.

name: Suloev Stretch
description: From a back ride on a standing or rising opponent, hook one of their legs with your arm behind the knee, extend your hips away, and straighten their leg against your chest to lock the hamstring and knee.
when_to_use: Use when they stand to shake off your back control — the standing leg you hook is the one carrying their weight, so the stretch arrives before they can base out of it. A rare answer to the single most common back-escape instinct at white belt.
source_notes: Named for Amar Suloev; kneebar-class legality applies.

name: Suplex (Ura Nage)
description: From a rear body lock, drop your hips below theirs, lift them with your legs while arching backward, and rotate mid-air to land chest-down past their shoulder in side control.
when_to_use: Use from a rear body lock when the mat return is defended by a wide base — the arch takes the base off the floor entirely. Competition note: finish with a controlled landing; spiking the head or landing them on the neck is illegal everywhere.
source_notes: Judo's ura nage and wrestling's suplex recorded as one row; controlled-landing rules apply.

name: Tarikoplata
description: Trap their arm in a kimura-style figure-four, then swing your near leg over the trapped shoulder and use the leg as the lever to rotate the shoulder instead of your arms.
when_to_use: Use when the kimura grip is set but their grip on their own belt or lapel is too strong to break by hand — the leg supplies the torque the arms could not. Finishes from guard, side control, or the scramble the kimura creates.
source_notes: Named for Tarik Hopstock; completes the -plata family beside Baratoplata and Monoplata.

name: Tripod Sweep
description: Grip one ankle, place the same-side foot on their hip and hook the other leg behind their far knee, then push the hip as you pull the ankle and lift the hook until they sit down backward — and stand up as they fall.
when_to_use: Use against a standing opponent reaching over your open guard — the three points of the tripod take their base in one direction while gravity supplies the rest. The guard-specific versions in this library are this technique wearing grips.
common_next_moves: Enter a takedown or guard pull
source_notes: The grip-agnostic fundamental behind the four guard-specific tripod sweeps already recorded.

name: Underhook Leg-Lock Escape
description: Sit up into the entanglement, underhook their top leg or reach a deep underhook on their torso, and drive your weight forward over your trapped knee until you can slide it free and come up on top.
when_to_use: Use while they are still organising the position — sitting into them collapses the space every leg lock needs. The escape doubles as a pass: the moment the knee clears, you are chest-to-chest with their guard already half beaten.
source_notes: The posture-and-pressure half of leg-lock defence; pairs with the heel-hook hand-fight row.

name: Von Flue Choke
description: When they hold a guillotine after you have passed to side control, drive your near shoulder into their neck, clasp your hands past their far shoulder, and walk your legs toward their head until the shoulder finishes the choke.
when_to_use: Use only when they keep a guillotine grip after the pass — the choke exists because their own grip pins their head to your shoulder. If they release the neck it disappears; that release is the point, and either answer wins.
source_notes: Named for Jason Von Flue; the standard punishment for a held guillotine.

name: Wrist Lock from Closed Guard
description: Trap their posting or gripping hand flat against your chest or collarbone, clasp both hands over the back of theirs, and crunch your chest toward the wrist to flex it past its range.
when_to_use: Use against a collar grip they refuse to release — the grip is the trap, because a gripping hand cannot slip free while it is still holding. Fast, quiet, and legal from blue belt; announce it in the gym before you own it.
source_notes: Completes the wrist-lock family, which covered side control, mount and back but not guard.

name: Mount Maintenance Against the Bridge
description: Ride the bridge rather than resisting it: post the hand on the mat over the direction of the roll, drop the head toward the same side, widen the knees, and let the hips fall back down as theirs return to the mat.
when_to_use: Use the moment the hips lift, before the trap-and-roll gets an arm and a leg on one side. Posting into the bridge is what makes the roll fail; squeezing the knees and holding still is what makes it work for them.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97); the supplied ordering names maintaining mount during bridging as its own lesson and the catalog held only static mount control.

name: Hook Insertion from Turtle
description: With the seatbelt already set, drive the near knee into the space behind their thigh, roll them onto the seatbelt-side shoulder, and thread the top hook in first so the second arrives as they turn.
when_to_use: Use once the seatbelt is connected and before they flatten out. The hook goes in on the side your chest is already on — chasing the far hook first is what feeds the roll-through and puts you underneath.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). Inserting the first hook is its own lesson in the supplied ordering; the catalog carried it only as an alias on Seatbelt Control from Turtle, which is a different skill.

name: Guillotine Defense
description: Drive the shoulder into the near side of their neck, walk your head to the choking-arm side so your throat leaves the crook of the elbow, strip the grip with both hands, and pass toward the free side.
when_to_use: Use the instant the chin is trapped, before they close guard or elevate the hips. Standing to relieve pressure works only while the legs are open; once the guard closes, moving to the choking-arm side is the whole answer.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). The supplied ordering asks for basic defense against eight named submissions; the catalog held no guillotine defense at all.

name: Triangle Defense
description: Get the trapped arm's shoulder across their throat, posture the head up, grip their far hip or shin to stop the angle, and stack toward the trapped shoulder while walking the free hand toward their hip.
when_to_use: Use before the legs lock and the angle is finished. The two things that end the danger are posture and denying the angle — pulling the trapped arm out first, without either, is what completes the lock.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). The catalog's only triangle answer was Mounted Triangle Escape, which is one specific position rather than the defense itself.

name: Armbar Defense
description: Turn the thumb toward the ceiling so the elbow points away from their hips, grip your own hands together, then stack forward over their shoulders and walk toward the trapped-arm side until the leg slips over your head.
when_to_use: Use the moment the leg crosses your face, while the arm is still bent. Once the arm is straight and the hips are elevated the answer is to tap — a defended armbar and a damaged elbow are seconds apart, which is why this belongs beside the attacks and not after them.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). The catalog held only Hitchhiker Escape from Armbar (Purple, mount-specific) and a Brown-belt counter.

name: Americana Defense
description: Straighten the trapped arm to take the bend out of the lock, walk the hand toward your own hip or under their body, and turn onto the trapped side to follow the shoulder rather than fighting it flat.
when_to_use: Use before the wrist is pinned to the mat and the elbow is walked down. Straightening the arm is what removes the lever — pulling straight up against their grip is a strength contest you are meant to lose.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). The americana is one of the first submissions a beginner meets and the catalog carried no defense for it.

name: Arm-Triangle Defense
description: Turn toward the trapped arm so the shoulder comes off your own neck, frame into their hip to stop them walking to the far side, and bridge into them before the head and arm are squeezed together.
when_to_use: Use while they are still on the near side. Once they have walked past the head and locked the shoulder against your neck the choke is already on, so the escape is a race against that walk, not against the squeeze.
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). Arm triangle appears three times in the supplied white belt ordering — twice as an attack, once as a defense — and only the attacks existed.

name: Straight Ankle Lock Defense
description: Flex the foot and point the toes toward their armpit so the blade of their forearm loses the Achilles, sit up toward the entangled leg, hand-fight their grip down, and pull the knee back out over the top.
when_to_use: Use as soon as the leg is entangled, before they fall back and finish the arch. Sitting up toward the lock is the answer; rolling away from it is the reflex, and it feeds the finish by turning your own leg into the lever.
setup_from: Straight Ankle Lock from Single-Leg X
common_counters: Follow the escape into a sweep
source_notes: Authored for the white belt roadmap (N97). The straight ankle lock is legal at every belt, so its defense belongs at white; the catalog held only Heel Hook Defense (Purple, no-gi only) and a Purple wrestle-up escape.

name: Knee-Cut Guard Recovery
description: Fight the underhook with a frame into the biceps, get the bottom shin back in front of their cutting knee, and either re-pummel the leg inside or take the far underhook and come up into the dogfight.
when_to_use: Use while the cutting knee is still on your thigh and the shoulder has not landed. Once they are chest-to-chest with the underhook the recovery is a half-guard fight, not a guard-retention one — which is the two answers this lesson pairs.
source_notes: Authored for the blue belt roadmap (N97). The supplied ordering names recovery against three specific passes; the catalog held generic retention only.

name: Toreando Guard Recovery
description: Turn the hips to face them as the legs are pushed aside, kick the trailing leg through to re-square, and reconnect a foot or a shin on the hip before they can put their weight down.
when_to_use: Use while they are still moving laterally and have not settled. The toreando beats you on speed, so the recovery is a rotation rather than a frame — trying to out-push the grips keeps the legs where they already are.
source_notes: Authored for the blue belt roadmap (N97); see knee-cut-guard-recovery.

name: Leg-Drag Guard Recovery
description: Before their hips settle on the dragged leg, turn into them and post on the far elbow, then either high-leg the top leg back over or turn to the knees and rebuild rather than staying flat.
when_to_use: Use in the moment between the drag and the weight arriving. A leg drag that is allowed to settle becomes a back exposure, so the choice here is spin back to guard or take the turtle deliberately — staying flat is what gives up the back.
source_notes: Authored for the blue belt roadmap (N97); named again at purple as recovering against the leg drag.

name: Body-Lock Pass Recovery
description: Attack the locked hands with a two-on-one before the hips are flat, get a knee or a shin back inside the lock, and turn to the side their head is on so the body lock has to be reset from the start.
when_to_use: Use before their hips connect and the lock closes below your own hips. Once the lock is set the retention window is gone and the work becomes a pin escape, which is why this is a purple-belt lesson rather than a blue-belt one.
common_counters: Ride the turn to the back
source_notes: Authored for the purple belt roadmap (N97). The supplied purple ordering names recovering against the body lock explicitly and the catalog had no entry.
